title: Indian-Origin US Lawmakers Urge Diaspora to Enter Politics as Anti-India Hate Rises
excerpt: At a Capitol Hill event, Congressmen Krishnamoorthi, Subramanyam and Thanedar called on Indian Americans to run for office at every level and fight back against a growing wave of anti-India rhetoric.
body:
• Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi told Indian Americans at a Capitol Hill event that they face "the rise of anti-Hindu, anti-Indian, anti-Desi hate" and must get more involved in politics than ever before.
  • Six Indian-American members of Congress — Krishnamoorthi, Bera, Jayapal, Khanna, Thanedar and Subramanyam — have issued joint statements condemning anti-India acts, including a flag-tearing incident in Frisco, Texas.
  • Republican Senator Roger Marshall highlighted the strategic importance of the India-US partnership, signalling bipartisan concern over the issue.
  • The Indian-American community, estimated at 5.2 million, is among the fastest-growing ethnic groups in the US but remains underrepresented in elected office.

Indian-American lawmakers from both parties are urging members of the diaspora to run for elected office and take a more active role in public life, warning that a surge in anti-India rhetoric demands a political response from the community itself.

At an event on Capitol Hill organised by the Foundation for India and Indian Diaspora Studies (FIIDS), Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi delivered a pointed call to action. Indian Americans, he said, are among the most educated and prosperous communities in the country — but that prosperity has not shielded them from a new wave of hostility.

"There is the rise of anti-Hindu, anti-Indian, anti-Desi hate. It's time to get more involved than you've ever been. You have to raise your voice. You have to speak up. You have to show up."

— Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL)

'If You Don't Have a Seat at the Table, You're on the Menu'

Krishnamoorthi urged community members to consider running for office at every level — city council, state legislature, US Congress — regardless of party affiliation.

https://x.com/IndiaToday/status/2081410173793607730

"I don't care if you're a Republican, Democrat, or Independent," he said. "There's an old saying in Washington DC: if you don't have a seat at the table, you're on the menu. And none of you can afford to be on the menu, nor can our families, nor can our interests."

Congressman Suhas Subramanyam echoed the message, saying representation in decision-making bodies is one of the most effective ways to address the challenges facing the community. Congressman Shri Thanedar warned that hate against immigrants is on the rise across the country and urged diaspora members to present a united front.

Bipartisan Support, but Growing Tensions

Republican Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas also addressed the event, emphasising the importance of the India-US partnership and calling for a bilateral trade deal that would benefit both countries. Several other Democratic lawmakers, including Sanford Bishop, James Walkinshaw, Brad Sherman and Bill Huizenga, assured support on immigration issues and the chronic green card backlog.

The bipartisan show of support comes against a backdrop of escalating tensions. President Trump amplified what Krishnamoorthi called "a racist rant attacking India and immigrants," prompting the House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats to accuse the president of "amplifying racist trash" on social media while the country faces serious geopolitical challenges.

From Frisco to San Francisco: A Pattern of Hostility

The lawmakers' push follows a string of anti-India incidents that have shaken the community. In June, a demonstrator at Frisco City Hall in Texas tore an Indian flag during an immigration-related protest while a crowd chanted anti-India slogans. The viral video prompted all six Indian-American members of Congress to issue a joint condemnation.

In California, Hindu temples have been repeatedly targeted. A Swaminarayan temple in Newark was defaced with anti-India graffiti, followed by a copycat attack on the Sherawali temple in Hayward just two weeks later. Hindus for Human Rights warned that what may appear as isolated incidents across Texas and California are "increasingly part of the same message: that temples, mosques, Indian families, Muslim families, and immigrant communities are not part of" America.

The Center for the Study of Organized Hate found that anti-Indian posts on X received more than 280 million views over a 10-week period, with content frequently framing Indians as "invaders" and "job thieves."

Diaspora Silence Under Scrutiny

The urgency of the lawmakers' message was reinforced by Congress MP Shashi Tharoor, who met a visiting delegation of US lawmakers and raised an uncomfortable question: why has the Indian-American diaspora been "so silent" about policies and rhetoric targeting India?

"One of the Congressmen said not one phone call has come to her office from any Indian-American voter asking her to support a change of policy. This is something that is surprising."

— Shashi Tharoor, Chairman of India's Standing Committee on External Affairs

What's Next

The Indian-American community, estimated at 5.2 million as of the 2023 US Census, is among the fastest-growing and most influential ethnic groups in the country, with increasing representation in business, academia and technology. But political representation has lagged. With just six members in Congress — all Democrats — the community's voice in the corridors of power remains disproportionately small relative to its economic and educational footprint.

Whether the current wave of anti-India hostility translates into greater political engagement from the diaspora remains to be seen. But the message from Capitol Hill is clear: showing up at the ballot box, and on it, is no longer optional.
